subject: surgery
title: Acute Suppurative Parotitis, Sialadenosis, and Salivary Imaging

steps.tx: In debilitated, dehydrated, or malnourished elderly patients recovering from major abdominal surgery, reduced salivary flow can precipitate **acute suppurative parotitis**. Historically called surgical parotitis, it develops when profound stasis in the parotid duct allows virulent oral bacteria to ascend in a retrograde manner from the mouth along Stensen duct into the parotid parenchyma. The predominant causative bacterial pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by oral viridans streptococci and anaerobes.
steps.say: Acute suppurative parotitis develops in dehydrated, postoperative elderly patients when poor salivary flow permits Staphylococcus aureus to migrate in a retrograde manner up Stensen duct.

nodes.label: Severe Reduction in Parotid Salivary Flow
Retrograde Bacterial Ascent Up Stensen Duct

steps.tx: A patient with acute suppurative parotitis presents with rapid onset of severe, throbbing preauricular pain, high-grade fever, systemic toxaemia, and exquisite swelling overlying the parotid region. The tense, unyielding fibrous parotid capsule restricts acute swelling, producing excruciating tenderness and marked trismus. Intraoral examination reveals an inflamed, edematous Stensen duct orifice opposite the upper second molar, from which **purulent discharge from Stensen duct** exudes on gentle external parotid massage.
steps.say: Patients experience severe preauricular pain, fever, and trismus. Massaging the swollen parotid gland reveals thick, purulent discharge milking out of Stensen duct orifice.

left.title: Acute Suppurative Parotitis
points: Rapid unilateral acute tender inflammatory swelling
Milking gland expresses thick frank pus from Stensen orifice
Requires vigorous intravenous hydration and targeted antibiotics

right.title: Viral Parotitis (Mumps)
points: Bilateral painful parotid swelling in pediatric patients
Stensen duct orifice is erythematous without purulence
Paramyxovirus infection accompanied by prodromal malaise
Self-limiting viral disease treated with supportive care

steps.tx: Massage over the swollen parotid here expresses cloudy pus from the duct papilla inside the cheek, confirming bacterial infection rather than simple obstruction. Finding **purulent discharge** at the orifice opposite the upper second molar anchors the diagnosis of acute suppurative parotitis at the chairside. Hydration, sialogogues and antistaphylococcal cover follow, with drainage reserved for fluctuance or failure to improve.
steps.say: Pus expressed from Stensen duct confirms acute suppurative parotitis. Hydration and antistaphylococcal treatment follow promptly.

vis.alt: Purulent discharge being milked from the Stensen duct orifice opposite the upper second molar
vis.caption: Purulent discharge milked from the Stensen duct orifice opposite the upper second molar. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Initial medical management of acute suppurative parotitis entails aggressive intravenous rehydration, warm local compresses, oral sialogogues such as lemon drops to stimulate salivary wash-out, and broad-spectrum intravenous antistaphylococcal antimicrobial therapy. If medical treatment fails to induce improvement within forty-eight to seventy-two hours, or if fluctuance is detected, surgical decompression is mandatory. Surgeons perform multiple horizontal incisions through the parotid capsule, carefully executing **surgical parotid drainage** parallel to facial nerve branches.
steps.say: Management includes vigorous rehydration, antistaphylococcal antibiotics, and sialogogues. If symptoms persist after three days, surgical decompression is performed parallel to the facial nerve.

rows: Intravenous Rehydration
Crystalloid infusion restoring intravascular circulating volume
Reverses dehydration and restores native serous salivary flow
Antimicrobial Therapy
Intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate or vancomycin for MRSA
Eradicates invasive Staphylococcus aureus and mixed oral flora
Sialogogue Stimulation
Sugar-free lemon drops, citrus fluids, and gentle massage
Mechanically flushes infected debris from obstructed ductal system
Surgical Capsular Decompression
Blair incision with horizontal capsular incisions parallel to CN VII
Relieves compartment pressure, drains microabscesses, prevents tissue necrosis

steps.tx: Not every swollen parotid is infected, and this painless bilateral enlargement proves the point. **Sialadenosis** fattens the glands with hypertrophied acinar cells in diabetes, alcoholism and eating disorders, without inflammation, fever or pus at the duct orifice. Mistaking it for suppurative parotitis buys antibiotics the patient never needed while the metabolic cause goes unexamined. The image's lesson is restraint: soft, painless, bilateral glands in a patient with a systemic reason should trigger a metabolic workup before an antimicrobial one.
steps.say: Sialadenosis is painless bilateral parotid enlargement from metabolic causes, not infection needing antibiotics.

steps.tx: In stark contrast to infectious or inflammatory disorders, **sialadenosis**, or sialosis, is a benign, non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic, painless bilateral swelling of the salivary glands, involving the parotid glands in over ninety percent of cases. Light microscopy reveals striking hypertrophy of serous acinar cells swollen with dense zymogen granules, unaccompanied by inflammatory infiltration or ductal dilatation. The pathophysiology represents an autonomic neuropathy disrupting intracellular secretory exocytosis.
steps.say: Sialadenosis is a benign, painless, non-inflammatory bilateral parotid enlargement. Driven by autonomic neuropathy, serous acinar cells become bloated with zymogen granules without inflammation.

vis.alt: Medical illustration showing bilateral symmetric parotid gland enlargement and salivary anatomy.
vis.caption: Bilateral parotid gland enlargement: non-inflammatory symmetric salivary expansion characteristic of sialadenosis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Because sialadenosis reflects underlying metabolic or autonomic dysfunction, establishing its etiology requires a comprehensive systemic evaluation. It is strongly linked to **chronic alcoholism with cirrhosis**, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, severe malnutrition, anorexia nervosa, and bulimia with frequent self-induced vomiting. Recognition of sialadenosis is essential to prevent unnecessary surgical biopsies or parotidectomies, as therapy is strictly medical, focusing entirely on correcting the underlying nutritional or metabolic derangement.
steps.say: Sialadenosis stems from systemic conditions like chronic alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, cirrhosis, and bulimia. Treatment focuses entirely on managing the underlying metabolic disorder, avoiding surgery.

rows: Endocrine & Metabolic
Diabetes mellitus and metabolic syndrome
Autonomic neuropathy with delayed acinar exocytosis of zymogen granules
Nutritional Disorders
Severe protein-calorie malnutrition and kwashiorkor
Metabolic deprivation causing compensatory acinar cell hypertrophy
Eating Disorders
Bulimia nervosa with recurrent self-induced vomiting
Autonomic overdrive triggered by gastric acid reflux and starvation
Hepatic & Toxic
Chronic alcohol abuse and alcoholic cirrhosis
Direct toxic autonomic neuropathy impairing salivary protein secretion

steps.tx: Radiological evaluation of the salivary ductal architecture has historically relied on **diagnostic sialography**. This radiographic examination involves direct retrograde cannulation of Stensen or Wharton duct orifice using a fine lacrimal probe, followed by the slow injection of water-soluble or lipid-based radiopaque iodinated contrast media under fluoroscopic control. Serial radiographs visualize ductal morphology, identifying radiolucent calculi, strictures, ductal diverticula, and glandular ectasias.
steps.say: Sialography visualizes the salivary duct tree by cannulating the duct opening and injecting radiopaque contrast. It identifies radiolucent calculi, duct strictures, and chronic dilatation.

rows: Suspected Sialolithiasis
Smooth, well-delineated filling defect with upstream ductal dilatation
Confirms location of radiolucent stone for sialendoscopy or extraction
Chronic Sialadenitis
Punctate sialectasis yielding snowstorm appearance
Documents ductal damage; managed conservatively with ductal washouts
Ductal Strictures
Localized smooth segment of caliber narrowing with proximal sausage dilatation
Amenable to balloon dilatation during interventional sialendoscopy
Salivary Fistula
Extravasation of radiopaque contrast into cheek soft tissue planes
Maps tract anatomy for surgical excision or botulinum toxin therapy

steps.tx: In chronic recurrent parotitis, sialography demonstrates characteristic spherical collections of contrast medium within dilated terminal ductules, producing a classic **punctate sialectasis**, often described as a snowstorm or string-of-sausages appearance. However, a rigid clinical rule governs this examination: sialography is absolutely contraindicated during active acute suppurative sialadenitis. Forceful retrograde injection of contrast into an acutely infected gland risks ductal rupture, severe pain, and catastrophic parenchymal extravasation.
steps.say: Sialography shows punctate sialectasis in chronic parotitis. However, it is strictly contraindicated during acute bacterial infection because pressure can rupture the infected duct system.

left.title: Indications for Sialography
points: Investigation of recurrent, unexplained salivary gland swelling
Detection and localization of non-calcified radiolucent stones
Evaluation of ductal stenosis, strictures, and sialectasis
Performed strictly during quiescent, asymptomatic intervals

right.title: Contraindications to Sialography
points: Active acute suppurative parotitis or sialadenitis
Documented clinical allergy to iodinated contrast media
Suspected acute parenchymal abscess with tissue necrosis
Pre-existing ductal transection or traumatic disruption

steps.tx: In contemporary head and neck surgery, invasive diagnostic sialography is increasingly supplanted by modern non-invasive imaging and interventional **salivary sialendoscopy**. Utilizing micro-endoscopes measuring zero point eight to one point three millimetres in outer diameter, surgeons navigate the ductal lumen under direct optical magnification. Diagnostic sialendoscopy allows immediate therapeutic intervention, such as wire-basket extraction of ductal calculi, balloon dilatation of fibrotic strictures, and localized intraductal corticosteroid lavage.
steps.say: Modern micro-sialendoscopy enables direct optical inspection of the duct lumen without radiation. Surgeons can extract stones using wire baskets and dilate strictures under direct vision.
